record.paper_title: Monetary Stabilization in Cryptocurrencies—Design Approaches and Open Questions
record.context_brief: Under-collateralized stablecoin loans and Sybil attacks
record.original_question: Can a permissionless cryptocurrency stablecoin implement under-collateralized loans—loans whose collateral value is lower than the value of the stablecoin loan—without allowing arbitrage through Sybil identities, or do such systems inevitably reduce to fully collateralized loans because borrowers can create fresh identities and abandon debt?

evidence.quote:
As discussed in Sec. IV, interest rates on deposits can
reduce the money supply only temporarily and thus should
be coupled with other techniques. When it comes to loans, an
interesting question is whether under-collateralized loans can
be implemented at all. This is the case in the regular economy,
where wealth or future income can be used as collateral. We
argue that this is impossible in permissionless cryptocurren-
cies due to the lack of strong identities and the resulting
vulnerability to Sybil attacks [7]. If under-collateralized loans
were implemented, rational actors would spawn multiple fake
identities to obtain loans and free money.
Theorem 1. In a permissionless setting without strong iden-
tities, under-collateralized loans enable arbitrage to the point
where only fully collateralized loans are available.

Even with smart contracts that enforce payments and in-
terest rates, the lack of strong identities makes it easy to
simply “exit-scam” the system, i.e., to generate a new debt-
free identity and start over without negative consequences.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a permissionless distributed payment system that issues a stablecoin (a token whose nominal value is pegged to some external reference). The system is permissionless in the sense that any participant may, at zero or negligible cost, create an arbitrary number of fresh pseudonymous identities (a Sybil capability), and there is no mechanism that binds an identity to a real-world entity, to off-chain wealth, or to verifiable future income.

The system offers collateralized loans: a borrower locks collateral of value C (denominated in the stablecoin's reference unit) and receives a loan of L stablecoins, subject to a smart contract that may enforce repayment schedules, interest, and liquidation of the collateral. A loan is called under-collateralized if C < L at the time of issuance, and fully collateralized if C ≥ L.

Assume borrowers are rational utility maximizers who may, at any time, abandon any identity (and any associated debt obligations not secured by on-chain collateral) and continue participating under a new identity at no cost.

Question: Is there any incentive-compatible loan-issuance mechanism implementable in this setting that allows under-collateralized loans (C < L) without enabling unbounded arbitrage by borrowers who create fresh Sybil identities, take out loans, and abandon the debt? Equivalently, must every such system in the permissionless, Sybil-vulnerable setting reduce to offering only fully collateralized loans (C ≥ L)?

Provide a proof that no such under-collateralized mechanism can exist, or exhibit a mechanism that achieves under-collateralization while remaining robust to Sybil exit-scam strategies.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an informal claim/theorem about permissionless stablecoins. While it is widely repeated in the cryptocurrency literature that Sybil attacks force on-chain loans to be over- or fully collateralized in the absence of strong identities, there is no universally accepted formal impossibility result; ongoing work on decentralized identity, reputation, soulbound tokens, and zero-knowledge KYC continues to explore partial workarounds. The status of a fully formal, model-independent impossibility theorem is best classified as unknown.
